summary: Procedural goal for 8–9 year-olds: plan and conduct a fair-test investigation that provides evidence of how balanced and unbalanced forces affect an object's motion. The craft is variable control (change exactly one of force number/size/direction, hold the rest constant), repeating readings, and then reading messy results to decide when forces are balanced (equal, opposite, no change in motion) versus unbalanced (motion changes). Science stays qualitative and relative (bigger/smaller pushes, not measured newtons); gravity is treated simply as a downward pull. The core experience should be a real hands-on investigation; a virtual investigation bench teaches the variable-control logic and is a strong complement but does not replace physically handling apparatus and real data.
misconceptions: 'Balanced forces' means there are NO forces / nothing is acting (balanced means equal and opposite, not absent)
Over-defaulting to 'fair test' as a slogan without grasping WHY only one variable may change (AKSIS: fair tests dominate primary practicals)
Changing more than one variable at once, or not repeating readings
Treating a prediction as a guess rather than reasoning from prior knowledge/evidence
The 'motion implies force' backbone — a moving object is thought to carry a force in its direction of travel
If a parachute/air-resistance context is used: that all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size or shape

activities.title: Run a real fair-test tug: how does the size of the pull change the motion?
steps: Set up a wheeled trolley at rest on a table, a string over a pulley at the table edge, a small pot you can add identical masses to, plus a metre ruler and stopwatch.
Choose ONE thing to change — the size of the pulling force (add masses one at a time) — and list everything you will keep the same: same trolley, same surface, same starting point.
Predict, using what you already know, what will happen as the pull grows, and say why (reason from prior knowledge, not a blind guess).
Run each setting at least three times, recording distance travelled in a set time (or speed) in a results table.

Point to a moment when the trolley was NOT changing its motion (for example, a setting where the pull was too small to move it, if your data has one) and say what the forces were doing; point to a moment when the motion WAS changing (for example, the trolley speeding up after starting from rest).
Use your own data to conclude whether a bigger pulling force produces a bigger change in motion.
activities.insight: Changing only one variable and repeating readings lets you read results as evidence: if the trolley starts at rest and a small pull leaves it still, that pull is balanced by friction, so the forces are balanced (no change in motion); once the pull is bigger than the friction the forces become unbalanced and the trolley starts to move and speed up toward the pull, and a bigger unbalanced force makes a bigger change in motion.

activities.title: Virtual investigation bench: lock the variables and see why only one may change
steps: On a virtual tug-of-war or cart-with-pushers bench (cart starting at rest), pick ONE independent variable (e.g. the force on the left); the bench keeps the others the same by default (same cart, same surface, same number of pulls), though you can unlock them to test what happens if you change more than one.
Run the trial three times and watch a results table fill in; note that with equal, opposite forces the two arrows match and the cart stays still.
Nudge one force bigger and observe the cart, starting from rest, begin to move toward that force; connect the unequal arrows (a resultant) to the motion changing.
Deliberately try to change two things at once and respond to the bench's prompt ('you changed the surface AND the force; which one caused it?').
State from the table when forces were balanced (equal, opposite, no change in motion) and when unbalanced.
activities.insight: The variable-control logic can be experienced, not just stated: equal and opposite forces produce no change in motion; an unequal pair produces a resultant that changes motion (here, from rest, the cart starts moving toward the larger force); and changing two things at once makes the cause unreadable.

activities.title: Sort and sequence the fair-test reasoning (retrieval companion)
steps: Put the steps of a fair test in order: question with one variable → decide what to change, measure, and keep the same → run repeated trials → read results → conclude.
Categorise described scenarios as balanced (no change in motion) or unbalanced (motion changing), including a still object held by a small pull cancelled by friction.
Answer 'which variable should you change, and which must stay the same?' prompts for a given question.
Explain in a sentence why repeating readings matters.
activities.insight: Fair-test reasoning can be rehearsed: one variable changes, the rest are controlled, readings are repeated, and balanced/unbalanced is judged by whether motion changes.

activities.title: Labelled tug-of-war reference scene (vocabulary scaffold)
steps: Study a labelled tug-of-war or cart scene; tap to reveal the force arrows in a balanced state (equal, opposite) and an unbalanced state (unequal, resultant).
Use a 'change one / keep the same' overlay to name the independent variable and the controlled variables for a chosen question.
Say aloud which state shows no change in motion and which shows motion changing.
activities.insight: Builds the set-up vocabulary and the look of balanced versus unbalanced force arrows before and alongside running a real test.

checkQuestion: Here is a wheeled trolley on the table, a string running over a pulley at the table's edge, a small pot you can add identical masses to, and a metre ruler and stopwatch. Plan and run a FAIR test to find out how the size of the pulling force changes how the trolley moves. Set it up, take your measurements, then use your results to point out a moment when the forces on the trolley were BALANCED and a moment when they were UNBALANCED.
checkAnswer: Changes only the pulling force (adds masses one at a time), keeps the trolley, surface and start point the same, and measures the effect on motion (distance in a set time, or speed), repeating readings. Reads the results as: while the trolley stays still and a small pull is cancelled by friction, the forces are balanced (no change in motion); once the pull is bigger than friction the forces are unbalanced and the trolley speeds up. Concludes a bigger unbalanced force makes a bigger change in motion.
